items: Broker tone turned incrementally more constructive at the infrastructure and data layer: BofA raised its infrastructure-software peer target multiple to 5.8x from 5.0x EV/CY27E revenue, while UBS procurement checks left application software as the funding source, not the beneficiary, of AI budgets.

Hybrid seat-plus-consumption pricing became the operating default this quarter — 50% of ServiceNow net-new business is now non-seat-based and Microsoft moved GitHub Copilot to usage pricing on June 1 — and the transition friction is surfacing first in bookings and renewals.

Company AI monetization kept accelerating against the cautious broker view: Microsoft AI ARR passed $37bn, up 123% y/y, and Salesforce agentic ARR passed $1bn; the layer-vulnerability ranking is unchanged with applications most at risk.

Credit migration continued: average non-accruals across JPM's 29-BDC universe rose 40bp QoQ to 2.46% of cost in 1Q26, and Morgan Stanley's broader universe average of 2.8% is a five-year high, with the sharpest sector rises in IT and healthcare.

The two largest losses of the software private-credit cycle crystallized in April — Medallia was handed to lenders in a $5.1bn equity wipeout and Affordable Care defaulted on a $1.4bn loan — yet JPM's credit team stayed overweight BDC debt as index spreads retraced to ~217bp.

Non-traded BDC redemption requests averaged 12.2% of NAV in 2Q against 5% caps that held everywhere; estimated net outflows of $3.1bn equal 2.56% of NAV, and KKR's $300mm support of FS KKR set the template for sponsor backstops.

Q2'26 NAV was $16.48, down $0.01 QoQ; non-accruals rose to 0.6% of cost from 0.3% on one small software addition while staying at 0.1% of fair value; GAAP NII of $0.30 covered 75% of the $0.40 distribution.

Net leverage rose to 0.93x from 0.85x — the first quarter inside the 0.90–1.25x target — funded by $500mm of new 6.50% Oct-2029 notes and $280mm of net SPV draws; PIK fell to 12.5% of investment income from 13.1%.

Litigation escalated from investigation notices to a filed complaint: a Section 36(b)<sup>1</sup> excessive-fee suit against the OTF adviser was filed June 18 in the S.D.N.Y., alleging inflated marks and fees charged on non-cash PIK accruals.

1.1 Key news on Blue Owl & OTF

items: First excessive-fee complaint filed directly against OTF's adviser. On June 18 two stockholders sued Blue Owl Technology Credit Advisors in the S.D.N.Y. under Section 36(b) of the Investment Company Act, alleging the adviser inflated asset marks to extract fees: advisory fees grew 191% from 2021 to 2025 against 134% asset growth, and fees are charged on PIK accruals that reached ~$43mm, about 25% of net investment income, in Q1'26. This escalates last quarter's plaintiff-firm investigation notices into discovery risk on OTF's Level-3 marks — though Section 36(b) plaintiffs have historically never prevailed at trial, so near-term economics are unchanged. Source: investmentnews.com

Q2'26 results, August 5: NAV $16.48 vs $16.49, NII $0.30, non-accruals 0.6% of cost and 0.1% of fair value, net leverage 0.93x, $55mm of stock repurchased in the quarter and ~$170mm over three quarters. The stock rose 7.4% on the print to $11.20, still ~0.7x NAV; management noted the discount implies roughly 40% portfolio defaults at 50-cent recoveries and expects lock-up-related selling to fade. Source: prnewswire.com

Second consecutive quarter of capped redemptions at Blue Owl's non-traded tech-credit funds, disclosed July 2: OCIC requests eased to 18.8% of shares from 21.9% and OTIC to 38.1% from 40.7%, $4.7bn combined vs $5.4bn in 1Q; both funds again honored only the 5% quarterly cap. OCIC holds $11.6bn of cash and capacity, about twelve quarters at the cap. The overhang on the franchise is stabilizing, not resolved; 3Q requests publish around early October. Source: semafor.com

OTF priced $500mm of 6.50% senior unsecured notes due October 2029 in early June; KBRA assigned BBB. Unsecured IG market access at a mid-6% coupon despite sector redemption stress is funding-side validation, at a cost of debt above much of the legacy stack. Source: businesswire.com

Moody's cut OCIC's outlook to negative on April 8, Baa2 affirmed, citing peer-high redemption requests and expected capital erosion — the first agency acknowledgment that the redemption run is a credit issue for Blue Owl's non-traded vehicles. No OTF-level rating action followed; the contagion channel to OTF is reputational and funding-cost, not direct. Source: alternativecreditinvestor.com

OCIC itself returned to the IG bond market on June 8 with $500mm of 5-year notes at roughly T+255, and Blue Owl Capital's Q2 results beat with shares recovering about 21% off the July lows — the manager-level franchise is proving more resilient than the redemption narrative implied. Source: bloomberg.com

Sell-side tail-risk framing persists: a July UBS note argued private credit defaults could reach ~15% in software-heavy funds, citing Blue Owl's $4.7bn of 2Q redemption requests. Single-source and unverified, but it keeps the software-credit narrative over the stock regardless of OTF's 0.1% fair-value non-accruals. Source: cryptobriefing.com

Medallia handed to lenders — a $5.1bn equity wipeout. Thoma Bravo agreed in late April to transfer the customer-experience software company, bought for $6.4bn in 2021, to creditors Blackstone, KKR, Apollo and Antares holding $3bn of debt; BDC marks on the loans sat at 74–79 cents beforehand. The largest software-LBO equity wipeout of the cycle, and direct evidence that 2021-vintage software buyout debt is where private credit losses are crystallizing — distressed software loans market-wide stood near $47bn. Source: in.investing.com

Affordable Care defaulted on a $1.4bn private credit loan in April, with Blackstone and KKR moving to take control of the dental-services provider bought by Harvest Partners for ~$2.7bn in 2021 — stress is not software-only; 2021-vintage healthcare-services unitranches are defaulting too. Source: privateequitywire.co.uk

KKR injected $300mm of sponsor capital into FS KKR alongside Q2 results — the first large explicit sponsor-support action of this downturn. JPM's credit team reads manager support of this kind as a sector-wide backstop; it is also an admission that BDC balance sheets need parent capital. Source: privateequitywire.co.uk

Marks moved at blue-chip platforms in Q2: Blackstone Secured Lending posted its largest quarterly NAV decline in six years with its bottom decile marked at 70 cents vs 73, and BlackRock TCP moved 48% of a $523mm loan pool into a continuation vehicle — liquidity engineering for credit tails is spreading and invites mark-management disputes. Source: privateequitywire.co.uk

The BDC litigation wave broadened beyond Blue Owl: a Section 36(b) suit against Ares Capital's adviser in May alleges fees up 53% to $773mm with look-through leverage of 2.06x vs the 1.12x headline, and securities class actions are pending against BlackRock TCP, Hercules and FS KKR — Level-3 marks and PIK-linked fees are now a sector-wide legal theme. Source: octus.com

The Q2 BDC reporting season read as stabilization, not resolution: non-accruals at cost rose at ARCC to 2.4% and OBDC to 2.8% while improving at FS KKR and Oaktree; origination stayed subdued, with Blue Owl vehicles repaying $747mm against $319mm of new commitments. Source: privateequitywire.co.uk

Enterprise software spend is being re-priced as tokenized labor: a leading model developer's revenue run-rate passed $30bn, from $9bn at end-2025, alongside managed-agent tooling that collapses the time to build enterprise agents; roughly $1.4tn of SaaS market value has repriced since early 2025 and the demand question for every application vendor is now which workflows agents absorb first. Source: cnbc.com

SaaS economics are being rewritten from the cost side: AI inference introduces genuine variable cost of goods into ~80%-gross-margin businesses — one marketing-tech company grew revenue 38% while costs rose 349% — pushing the industry toward a transitional Rule of 30 as vendors reinvest against AI-native entrants; margin durability, not growth, becomes the variable to underwrite. Source: bain.com

The offensive case for incumbents was quantified at ~$100bn in the US alone: agentic AI that automates cross-system labor — the human coordination between ERP, CRM, billing and ticketing that rules-based automation never captured — converts labor budgets into software spend, and vendors holding proprietary workflow data are best positioned to capture it. Source: bain.com

Research across 45 public SaaS companies concluded the build-vs-buy shift is real but uneven: AI coding tools let enterprises rebuild commodity workflow software in-house, while SaaS powered by pooled cross-customer data performing predictive tasks retains pricing power — software credit should be sorted by data moat and task type, not treated as one risk bucket. Source: hbr.org

Software producers themselves are restructuring: revenue at leading software companies grew 22% faster than headcount over the past year, and the standard 7–9-person engineering squad is giving way to 3–5-person hybrid-agentic pods — structurally lower headcount intensity, and lower seat counts for the tools sold into those teams. Source: bain.com

Monetization began moving from seats to agent consumption: major platforms started billing directly for agent usage and standing up enterprise agent-governance layers during the quarter — an early template for recapturing value when the user is software, and an accelerant of the industry-wide shift toward usage and outcome pricing. Source: techtimes.com

The AI-software story formally crossed into credit: major financial press mapped how private equity and private credit concentrated in software ahead of the AI shock, connecting agent-substitution risk to the ~$47bn distressed software-loan stack — AI is now an underwriting variable in leveraged software credit, not just an equity theme. Source: bloomberg.com

blocks.html: Net leverage ended Q2'26 at 0.93x, up from 0.85x in Q1'26 — the first quarter inside the management target range of 0.90x–1.25x since listing. The increase was deployment-led rather than write-down-led: $478mm of net funded investment activity was financed with the new unsecured notes and SPV draws while net assets were flat, and asset coverage remained comfortable at 203% against the 150% statutory floor, although down from 226% at year-end 2025. From here the fund retains roughly $2.4bn of debt capacity to the top of the target range, equivalent to about a third of current net assets, which is the principal forward driver of NII per share while base rates are flat. Symmetrically, the cushion to the regulatory floor is wide: net assets would have to absorb roughly $4.0bn of portfolio value decline, about 27%, before the 150% test binds.

items: BofA maintained Neutral with an unchanged $11.50 price objective at ~0.7x NAV after Q2 results, having cut from $14.00 in May. The house titled the quarter Stable — NAV flat at $16.48 and portfolio yield up 10bp to 9.3% — after Q1's Challenging quarter framing, so the negative-revision cycle paused. Adjusted core EPS of $0.30 rose 3% QoQ, one cent below the $0.31 consensus but above the broker's own $0.28 on stronger interest and dividend income; standing core EPS estimates for 2026 and 2027 remain $1.21 and $1.26 with no new revision published. On credit the note counts non-accruals of 0.6% at cost across two issuers — one software addition, one exit — among the lowest in the industry, and flags PIK declining to 12.5% of revenue, substantially all original-underwrite. The core argument for staying at Neutral despite the discount: credit is pristine and the outlook slowly improving, but core profitability will lag peers for the near future given significant excess capital. Versus last quarter the rating, objective and multiple are unchanged and the tone shifted from yield-pressure caution to stabilization.

blocks.html: This quarter confirms that the sector's NAV drawdown is a valuation reset, not yet a credit-cycle break — but the credit dispersion beneath it widened materially. Every one of the six NAVs fell or held over the first half with the declines still dominated by spread marks — ARCC's Q2 NAV slipped 1.2% while its NII covered the dividend at 104%, and TSLX and GBDC earned their reset payouts in full — yet the quarter also produced the cycle's first genuinely idiosyncratic credit prints: BXSL's cost-basis non-accruals jumped from 0.6% to 3.6% almost entirely on Medallia, GBDC's reached 2.9% across twenty issuers including preferred positions, and three of the six cut distributions.

Fee mechanics have entered a non-linear zone

blocks.html: Two fee breakpoints now sit close to current operating levels. First, the management fee steps from 1.50% to 1.00% on average gross assets below a 200% asset-coverage ratio; OTF ended the quarter at 203%, so nearly all incremental leverage from here is charged at the lower 1.00% marginal rate — a modest but real offset to the cost of the leverage build. Second, the income incentive fee moved to the post-listing schedule of 17.5% above a 1.5% quarterly hurdle, with the catch-up completing at 1.82% of NAV per quarter. Q2 pre-incentive income ran at roughly 2.2% of opening NAV, safely in the 17.5% marginal zone, but a decline of about 18% in quarterly NII would drop the fund into the catch-up band, where each marginal dollar of income accrues entirely to the adviser. With base coverage at 86%, this non-linearity deserves a standing line in the quarterly review; the capital-gains incentive accrual was zero this quarter after Q1's $38.8mm reversal.

items: Software and AI exposure is the sector's defining fault line, but the stress to date is idiosyncratic and concentrated — Medallia alone accounted for 26% of all 1Q26 non-accrual additions at cost — rather than systemic.

Fundamentals are directionally worsening off a manageable base: non-accruals at multi-year highs on every universe measured, PIK elevated, and NAV declines driven predominantly by spread marks rather than realized losses.

Redemption pressure at non-traded funds is a liquidity event, not a solvency event: 5% caps held everywhere in 2Q, net outflows were about 2.6% of NAV against far larger bank-line and liquid-asset buffers, and public-market funding reopened.
The 2028 software maturity wall — not current payment default — is the operative catalyst all four houses watch; refinancing friction is where AI-era credit stress will first crystallize.
Recovery pessimism on software credit is viewed as overdone: posited recoveries of 70–80% on smaller lender groups, and realized software recoveries since 2016 track overall first-lien rates.

blocks.html: Private middle-market leverage has been de-levering for three years while its public comparable re-levered. Fitch's monitored private portfolio sits at 5.9x, down a tenth QoQ and roughly a full turn below the near-6.9x peak of late 2022, while the Lincoln valuation sample has been remarkably stable at 5.2x inside a 4.8–5.2x band across the whole period. The line that has actually moved against the trend is the gray one: single-B public loan borrowers have re-levered from a 5.1x trough to 5.5x, so the private-versus-public gap has narrowed from about 1.7 turns at the 2022 peak to 0.4 turns on the Fitch measure — and on the Lincoln sample private borrowers now carry 0.3 turns less leverage than comparable public issuers. The read for OTF is that the aggregate borrower entering this credit cycle is less levered than the one that entered 2023, so the sector's rising non-accruals are not being driven by balance-sheet gearing at the median. Where gearing does bite is sectoral: software borrowers run a median 8.3x against the 7.0x all-sector figure on the S&P credit-estimate universe, i.e. more than two turns above the Fitch median shown here, concentrated precisely in the end-market that dominates OTF's book.

blocks.html: Coverage tells the opposite story to leverage — it collapsed through the hiking cycle and has only partly healed. Fitch's private median troughed at 1.56x in early 2024 and has recovered to 2.0x; Lincoln troughed at 1.36x and is back to 1.9x. Both remain roughly 0.8 turns below their 2021–22 levels and still sit under the 2.5x public single-B benchmark, so the typical direct-lending borrower continues to profile like a low-single-B credit on cash-flow cushion even after four quarters of improvement. The mechanism matters for forecasting: this recovery is base-rate driven rather than earnings driven — falling SOFR cut cash interest expense on floating-rate loans, the same move that compressed OTF's asset yields from 10.4% to 9.6% over five quarters. That symmetry is the key point for the portfolio: the rate path that repairs borrower coverage is the same one that erodes OTF's investment income, so improving borrower fundamentals and falling NII are two views of one variable rather than offsetting signals. It also means the cushion is fragile — a stall in cuts halts the coverage repair with the median still under 2.0x.

blocks.html: Measured against net investment income the same PIK dollars look far heavier — 15.2% in Q1'26 versus 6.4% on the gross basis — because NII is struck after interest and management expenses, so the ratio is geared. This is the more decision-relevant cut for a dividend-paying vehicle: it says roughly one dollar in seven of the sector's distributable earnings is accrued rather than collected. The trend here is clearly upward where the gross measure was flat, rising about 2.8pp from 12.4% at Q1'23 to 15.2% now, with the Q1'26 print the second-highest of the series and down only 0.4pp from the Q4'25 high. blocks.html: The sector decomposition explains where the aggregate deterioration came from and why it matters more for OTF than OTF's own 0.6% print suggests. Information technology's non-accrual rate tripled against its three-year average, to 2.1% from 0.7%, and healthcare's doubled to 3.5% — now the highest of any sector — while financial services and energy actually improved, to 0.5% and 0.1%. IT also posted the worst average quarterly write-down at −2.7% and the highest share of sub-90 PIK loans at 8.4% against a 3.7% three-year average, so marks, PIK stress and non-accruals all point at the same two sectors rather than disagreeing. Those two sectors are OTF's book: systems and application software are 32.8% of fair value, health care technology a further 12.4%, and health care providers 2.9% — roughly 48% of the portfolio sits in the two end-markets driving the sector's credit migration. This is the transmission channel to watch, and it operates through marks and spreads well before it reaches non-accruals: sector-wide software and healthcare stress re-prices OTF's Level-3 valuations and its equity discount whether or not its own borrowers miss a payment.

The core test of durable value per layer has shifted from “is it sticky” to “the quality of stickiness” — good stickiness built on continuous innovation and high-frequency genuine usage endures; bad stickiness maintained by switching costs and contractual lock-in erodes.

blocks.text: Vulnerability ranking: Application/Record > Orchestration/Intelligence ≈ Data/Platform > Infrastructure

items: The application/record layer is most fragile — systems of record capture only ~5% of decision-relevant information, and ~99% of relevant customer intelligence never enters the system of record; value is most easily lifted into the intelligence layer above, especially for vendors relying purely on seats and switching costs (GS).

The orchestration/intelligence and data/platform layers sit in the middle — value recipients, yet exposed to entry-point competition and commoditization; they need data assets and governance as a second moat.
The infrastructure layer is most resilient — AI workload volume directly drives demand, least exposed to budget rationalization, with demand driven by incremental usage rather than price increases.

blocks.html: Marginal change: application/services pricing reconstruction most acute > infrastructure/data demand acceleration > orchestration entry points opening

items: The sharpest marginal change is pricing reconstruction in the application/services layer — from pure seats to seat+consumption and even outcome-based pricing; the transition is long and friction-heavy, only vendors delivering quantifiable savings can raise prices, and mature seat-priced applications are hit hardest.

Next is demand acceleration in the infrastructure/data layer — larger attack surfaces lift security demand, machine-generated code volume lifts data, governance and observability demand, and consumption pricing scales naturally with workloads.

Entry points in the orchestration/intelligence layer are opening — intelligent-OS/ontology layers, headless calls and open agent protocols expand the surfaces through which intelligence is consumed; first movers accumulating proprietary data assets benefit.

items: Software value migrates from the record layer to the orchestration/intelligence layer, and further down into the data/platform and infrastructure layers — the application/record layer is the value donor, not the recipient.

Beneficiaries: owners of underlying technical moats and proprietary data assets — the data/platform and infrastructure/security layers, plus intelligence-layer vendors able to compound unstructured interactions into data assets and monetize headless calls.

Pressured: pure-record front-office/application software held together by switching costs and seat lock-in — model intelligence itself is only ~10% of the value; the moat is not the model but context, workflow, governance and data.
